outcome: Answered yes for the standard two-player 52-card game: Brayden Casella's balanced deal (reported 10 Feb 2024; arXiv preprint 19 Mar 2024; The American Mathematical Monthly 2025) loops forever, with a 62-trick cycle reachable from 30 balanced starting deals; a 2026 arXiv preprint by Andorno, Cernoia, Duiz and Michelangeli adds further non-terminating deal families. The live Wikipedia list, as fetched on 12 Oct 2026, no longer shows the bullet, though the frozen 26 Jan 2024 snapshot does.
problem_asks: One existence question: is there a starting deal, under the game's rules, from which play never terminates? The statement names no deck, no number of players and no penalty rules. On the default reading (two players, standard 52-card deck with four each of J, Q, K, A, standard penalties of 1, 2, 3 and 4 cards for J, Q, K, A) that is the whole question. It has no quantitative part: no count of such deals and no bound on game length. The Wikipedia wording is 'Is there a non-terminating game of beggar-my-neighbour?' under Games and puzzles (frozen snapshot, data/will-2026-10-10-haiku/page.wiki line 185, with {{Main|Game theory}} above it and no sub-bullets).

events.what_happened: Marc M. Paulhus, 'Beggar My Neighbour', The American Mathematical Monthly 106(2), 1999, pp. 162-165, in the journal's Unsolved Problems section. Cited in the Casella et al. reference list and in Andorno et al. 2026. Andorno et al. say that [8] in their reference scheme 'identified loops only in smaller, modified deck configurations, such as N=24 with two rather than four special cards for each type'. I did not confirm that [8] is Paulhus, and I did not open the article: the softbank copy refused connection and JSTOR was not tried.
events.delivers: Per second-hand reports only: non-terminating loops in reduced or modified deck configurations (N=24 with two special cards per type). Nothing reported about the standard 52-card, 26-26 deal.
events.remains: The standard two-player 52-card question, as far as the reported content goes.
events.direction: Does not answer the bullet in the standard game as far as reported. If the reported reduced-deck loops are as Andorno et al. describe, it is a neighbouring question (different deck), not the bullet's.
events.object: Second-hand description only: loops in reduced decks, e.g. N=24 cards with two special cards of each type. Not read directly, so whether the object is explicit is unknown.

events.what_happened: A. Aleksenko and E. Lakshtanov, 'Finiteness of the playing time in Beggar-my-neighbour card game', arXiv:1109.1460, v1 7 Sep 2011, v2 6 Dec 2011; journal publication Problems of Information Transmission 49(2), 2013, pp. 163-166. The abstract proves that the expected playing time is finite in Beggar-my-neighbour-type card games when the starting player is chosen at random and the deck is shuffled as each trick is added, for the generic setting of the game. The abstract does not mention non-terminating or infinite games.
events.revisions: v1 7 Sep 2011; v2 6 Dec 2011 (per arXiv abs page); journal version 2013.
events.delivers: Finite expected game length, but only under two randomisations: a random starting player and reshuffling as each trick is added. It says nothing about any particular deterministic deal.
events.remains: All of the bullet: existence of an infinite deterministic deal is not addressed.

checked_by.qualification: refereed journal publication; referee details not read
checked_by.where: https://arxiv.org/abs/1109.1460 (journal reference given on the abs page)

events.direction: Does not bear on existence of infinite deterministic games. It answers a different, randomised question, and the abstract is explicit about its scope.

events.what_happened: A 2023 GitHub pull request comment (see gentilini-2023-pr-camicia) says that the Italian card game Camicia, played with a 40-card deck, 'was declared non terminating in 2016b and in 2017c'. The comment cites a Computer Science Stack Exchange answer ('Does this game terminate?', undated on the page) and a text file dated 20170217 in the drago-96/cavacamisa GitHub repository. I did not open either cited source. The dates and what was declared are second-hand, and the Wikipedia article's footnote 9 points to the same PR title.
events.delivers: Per the claim only: infinite play in a 40-card variant (Camicia). Nothing about the 52-card game.
events.directly_checkable: Per the claim only: a Camicia starting deal that loops, which I did not obtain or check.
events.doubts: The claim rests on a Stack Exchange answer and a 2017 file I did not open. The 2023 commenter reports that his own C++ code confirmed it, which is an unpublished check.
events.direction: Affirmative, but for a different game (40-card Camicia). It does not answer the 52-card question. It would answer the bullet only on a reading that counts Camicia as 'a game of beggar-my-neighbour' (see disputes).

events.what_happened: Reed Nessler's longest terminating game record: 1164 tricks and 8344 turns (cards played). The Casella et al. arXiv Appendix A lists it dated 09-06-2022 (day-month order, so 9 June 2022); the Wikipedia article gives the same record as of February 2024. Nessler's Baylor page and the Mann records page were seen only through search summaries and the Wikipedia text. This is a finite-game record, not a result on infinite play.
events.delivers: A terminating game of 1164 tricks (8344 turns). It is not a result about infinite play.
events.remains: The whole bullet. The record bears on a neighbouring question (longest terminating game), which the Wikipedia article and the Casella paper mention as context.
events.direction: Does not cut either way on existence of a non-terminating game. It is a finite record on a different question, discounted.

events.what_happened: Alessandro Gentilini opens pull request #5, 'Add a finiteness test', on matthewmayer/beggarmypython (opened 9 Mar 2023, merged 8 Jun 2023, per the page). He proposes a finiteness test for the Beggar-my-neighbour simulator, says he is not fully sure it is correct, says his own C++ code had confirmed that Camicia is infinite, quotes 'Camicia was declared non terminating in 2016b and in 2017c', and quotes Paulhus (1999) that a billion random Camicia deals produced no cycle. The PR body I read gives no starting deal.
events.delivers: A claim that the 40-card Camicia has infinite games, supported by the author's own unpublished code; and a finiteness test for the simulator. The test is not a proof of anything in the bullet.

checked_by.what_they_did: merged the finiteness-test PR on 8 Jun 2023; the page does not show him checking the Camicia claim

events.doubts: The author says he is not fully sure his test is correct. The Camicia infinite claim rests on his unpublished C++ code and on the 2016/2017 sources I did not open.
events.direction: Affirmative for the 40-card Camicia variant only. Not an answer on the 52-card game.

events.what_happened: Richard Mann's beggar-my-neighbour records page has an entry, dated 10-02-2024 (day-month-year), 'An infinite game of Beggar-My-Neighbour has been found!', found by Brayden Casella: deal Player 1 ---K---Q-KQAJ-----AAJ--J--, Player 2 ----------Q----KQ-J-----KA, 'Game loops after 474 turns and 66 tricks', with a link to the arXiv paper. Wikipedia gives the same date ('reported on 10 February 2024'). The HLF post (Steckles, Aug 2024) says Casella 'shared' the deal in February 2024, and that a Mastodon bot posted it. The records page entry is a posting of the deal and loop length, with no argument; the argument is the 19 Mar 2024 preprint.
events.revisions: Page revision date not established; the entry is later linked to arXiv 2403.13855.
events.delivers: A report of one balanced two-player 52-card deal that, under the standard rules, enters a loop after 474 turns and 66 tricks, so play never ends (the page's claim). It gives no argument beyond the loop length.
events.remains: The bullet's question is answered by this claim if it is verified. The 30-deal family and the 62-trick cycle come from the arXiv event.
events.directly_checkable: Yes. The deal is written out in the entry and the game is deterministic, so a simulator or a hand run can check that the position recurs after 474 turns. I did not run one.
events.direction: Affirmative: a deal that never ends in the standard game, as the page claims.
events.object: An explicit deal: Player 1 ---K---Q-KQAJ-----AAJ--J--, Player 2 ----------Q----KQ-J-----KA (26 cards each). The letters are face cards and the dashes are non-face cards; I checked this by counting, since the two hands together hold four of each of K, Q, A, J and 36 non-face cards. Per HLF, the first 34 cards are not part of the loop; after 474 turns and 66 tricks (33,034 cards played) the game returns to the state after the 34th card. The entry is an explicit example, not an existence proof.
people: Richard P. Mann (maintains the records page; co-author of the paper)

events.what_happened: Casella, Anderson, Kleber, Mann, Nessler, Rucklidge, Williams and Wu, 'A Non-Terminating Game of Beggar-My-Neighbor', arXiv:2403.13855, v1 submitted 19 Mar 2024 (18:56 UTC), submitted by R. Mann; no later arXiv version listed on the abs page. The paper gives a balanced two-player 52-card deal (26 cards each) whose play reaches a cycle, a 62-trick cycle reached after 4 tricks, and identifies 30 distinct starting deals that reach the same cycle. The construction uses a backward method ('Casella's Ansatz') that combines pieces ending in jacks and plays back from the loop to find a balanced deal, with computer search for pieces and modifications. Appendix D gives a 62-trick trace. Accepted by The American Mathematical Monthly 25 Nov 2024; published online 20 Oct 2025; print vol. 132 no. 10, pp. 978-994; DOI 10.1080/00029890.2025.2558484 (per White Rose record). The journal text was not readable to me (403).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (19 Mar 2024). Accepted 25 Nov 2024 (eprints deposit 26 Nov 2024); Monthly published online 20 Oct 2025, print 26 Nov 2025 per the White Rose record. The accepted manuscript and the published text differ from v1 by unknown amounts; I read only the arXiv v1 HTML.
events.delivers: Existence, in the standard two-player 52-card game (26 cards each, standard penalties), of starting deals under which play never ends: a 62-trick cycle reached from 30 distinct balanced starting deals, entered after 4 tricks (474 turns in total, per the records page). Restrictions: two players, the 52-card deck with four of each face card, the standard penalty rules, and balanced 26-26 deals. Silent on other player counts, other deck sizes and other rule sets. The result is a single explicit family, with a constructive method, not a full classification of infinite deals.
events.remains: Nothing of the bullet as worded. The paper's closing questions, per a search summary (not verified in text I could read), concern how many non-terminating games exist and the longest possible terminating game; neither is part of the bullet.

events.directly_checkable: Yes. The two 26-card hands are written out in the paper and on the records page, and the game is deterministic, so anyone can simulate it under the standard rules: the state after the 34th card recurs at 474 turns / 66 tricks. Appendix D gives a 62-trick trace of the cycle. Open-source simulators exist (BeggarMyPython per the HLF post; GitHub repositories found by search), but I did not run any of them.
events.direction: Affirmative: the standard two-player 52-card game has non-terminating deals. This is the answer the question asks for.
events.object: An explicit family of balanced 52-card deals: Player 1 ---K---Q-KQAJ-----AAJ--J--, Player 2 ----------Q----KQ-J-----KA, and 29 others that reach the same cycle (30 in all, per the abstract). The cycle is 62 tricks long, entered after 4 tricks; in total the loop recurs at 474 turns and 66 tricks. The objects are finite, deterministic and checkable by simulation, and they are explicit deals, not a non-constructive existence proof. The construction is constructive but uses computer search for the pieces; the paper says a 'large part of the search' was brute force.
people: Brayden Casella (lead author; credited with the discovery)
Richard P. Mann (University of Leeds per the White Rose record; submitted the arXiv version)

events.what_happened: Nicolas Andorno, Giulio Cernoia, Simone Duiz, Alessandro Michelangeli, 'The Dynamical Landscape of Beggar-My-Neighbour: Ultra-long Matches, Loops, and Infinite Matches', arXiv:2602.23406, v1 submitted 26 Feb 2026. Treats the game as a deterministic dynamical system; studies the split between terminating and non-terminating matches and the approximately exponential tail of finite match lengths; introduces an 'Infinite Loop Factory' algorithm (adaptive insertion, backtracking, up to 1500 checkpoints) that finds non-terminating cycles from balanced initial decks in the standard (52,4) setting and in generalised settings; a section 'Dynamical landscape and open problems' (Section 13). Says a 1-in-150,000 claim is 'false' (see disputes).
events.revisions: v1 26 Feb 2026 (abs page). The abs page lists v2 as revised 2 Jul 2026; the HTML page labels v2 as dated 24 Aug 2026. The two dates conflict and I have not resolved them.
events.delivers: Further instances of non-terminating play: additional balanced standard (52,4)-deck families generated by the algorithm, and non-terminating matches in generalised deck configurations. It confirms 'Non-terminating matches for Beggar-My-Neighbour do, in fact, exist'. It adds instances of the same existence type. It does not change the answer to the bullet, which Casella et al. already give for the standard game.
events.remains: Nothing of the bullet as worded. The open problems in its Section 13 concern a taxonomy of decks, the dynamical landscape, backward determinism and the existence window for loops, none of which is the bullet.
events.directly_checkable: The loops are deterministic and can be checked by simulation. The paper refers to a C-script for the loop factory; I did not obtain or run it.
events.direction: Affirmative, and extends the affirmative answer to more deals and to generalised decks. It does not move any quantity the bullet asks about beyond existence.
events.object: Further explicit balanced deal configurations and their loops, produced by the Infinite Loop Factory. I did not read the list of configurations (a search summary says a table is given). Each is a finite deterministic cycle checkable by simulation. Explicit, not non-constructive.

disputes.summary: Scope and priority for the Camicia claims. Gentilini (2023 PR, citing 2016b and 2017c declarations) and the Wikipedia article ('some smaller decks of cards have infinite games, such as Camicia') say the 40-card Camicia has infinite games. If the bullet's 'a game of beggar-my-neighbour' includes that variant, the question was answered before 26 Jan 2024 and Casella's 2024 deal is not the first answer. The 52-card reading is the one Casella et al. answer, and the frozen list treats the question as open, which supports that reading. Judging pass to decide.

Andorno et al. (arXiv 2602.23406) say it 'has frequently been claimed (for instance in [1, 9, 5, 4]) that infinite (52,4)-matches were found in [8] with a frequency of approximately 1 in 150,000', call this a 'chain of misreporting in the literature' and say 'Both assertions are false'; [8] identified loops only in smaller, modified deck configurations such as N=24 with two special cards per type. I could not identify [8] or the four citing works. The 1-in-150,000 figure is attributed to Berlekamp, Conway and Guy only in a secondary search summary (an Integers paper I could not open, 503). No primary source located, so this claim is undated and is recorded here, not as an event.

summary: The question has an affirmative answer in the standard two-player 52-card game. Brayden Casella is credited with the discovery. The earliest dated report I found is the entry on Richard Mann's beggar-my-neighbour records page dated 10 Feb 2024 (the entry is a deal and a loop length, with no argument). The Wikipedia article gives the same date. The written argument is the arXiv preprint 2403.13855 (v1 19 Mar 2024, the only arXiv version), which gives a balanced 26-26 deal whose play enters a 62-trick cycle reached from 30 starting deals; the paper was accepted by The American Mathematical Monthly on 25 Nov 2024 and published online 20 Oct 2025 (vol. 132 no. 10, pp. 978-994, DOI 10.1080/00029890.2025.2558484). Sources for the paper: I read the arXiv abs page and the arXiv v1 HTML in full section coverage through a summariser, and the White Rose record. The arXiv PDF returned unreadable binary, the White Rose accepted manuscript returned 401, and the Taylor and Francis page returned 403, so the published text, its acknowledgements and its referee credits are unverified. The construction is computer-assisted (brute force over balanced games up to 26 cards; random search for decks up to 42 cards in the paper's history section) but I found no AI system named anywhere in the arXiv text I read, and the paper has no acknowledgements section. Independent engagement: Andorno, Cernoia, Duiz and Michelangeli (arXiv 2602.23406, 26 Feb 2026) cite the Monthly paper as [2], treat its existence result as established, and give further balanced 52-card loops from their own 'Infinite Loop Factory' algorithm. Their paper also calls a 1-in-150,000 claim false. Popular digests: Steckles (HLF SciLogs, 2024), Britton (blog, Jan 2025), and an Aperiodical year-end roundup (Dec 2024, seen only as a search snippet). I checked the Wikipedia list in three ways: the frozen 26 Jan 2024 snapshot has the bullet under Games and puzzles (line 185); the live list as fetched today shows no beggar-my-neighbour bullet in that section; and the edit history I could reach covers only 11 Sep to 10 Oct 2026, with no edit summary mentioning the bullet, so the removal date is undated. AI search: I ran six AI-specific searches (AI model, LLM, GPT-5 Pro / Claude / Gemini Deep Think, AlphaEvolve / ChatGPT / Gemini, 'non-terminating card game discovered by AI', Lean formalisation) and found no source crediting an AI system with any part of the result, and no Lean formalisation. Close calls for the judging pass: (a) the first public item is the 10 Feb 2024 records entry, while the first written argument is the 19 Mar 2024 preprint; both are after the frozen revision, so the window is unaffected, but which one is the event is a call for later; (b) the scope of 'a game of beggar-my-neighbour' (see disputes): the 40-card Camicia claims of 2016/2017 are secondhand and unverified, and Paulhus (1999) reports reduced-deck loops; (c) the 1-in-150,000 claim is undated and disputed by its critics. Nothing I found shows an error in the Casella deal or cycle, and none of the critics engaged with the 52-card construction itself.
competing_reading: The bullet names no deck or player count. Read generally, the question was answered before the window: Paulhus (1999) reported loops in reduced decks, and the 40-card Camicia has been reported infinite since 2016/2017. On that reading the 2024 deal is not the first answer, and the 2024 event would not change the question's status. Against it: the frozen Wikipedia list treats the question as open, the Casella et al. paper, Conway's remark and the Wikipedia article all frame the question on the standard game, and the Paulhus and Camicia claims are secondhand or unread by me.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The published Monthly text (acknowledgements, any AI-use or software statement, referee acknowledgements) and the accepted manuscript, both of which were unreachable. (2) The Paulhus 1999 article, to confirm which deck it covers and whether it posed the question. (3) The 2016b/2017c Camicia sources (the Stack Exchange answer and the 2017 repository file), to date the claim. (4) The primary source for the 1-in-150,000 figure and the identity of [8] in Andorno et al. (5) The edit history of the live list before 11 Sep 2026, to date the removal of the bullet and to see the edit summary. (6) Checking the deal in a simulator, to confirm the 474-turn loop independently of the paper.
